A novel approach has been developed to simulate the Alfvén wave parametric decay instability in a plasma, utilizing a hybrid model that combines kinetic theory for ions with fluid theory for electrons. This model can accurately represent the characteristics of very low frequency Alfvén waves in a plasma, taking into account the low frequency and low temperature of electrons. By incorporating a kinetic treatment for ions and a fluid treatment for electrons, this model can effectively describe the instability and its effects on ion energy distribution. It has been shown that the model can replicate the key features of this instability, including the decay of a high-energy wave into two or more lower-energy waves, and can be used to study the growth of this instability in a plasma.

We examine the gravitational instability in thread-like molecular nebulae, which are modeled as non-circular, rotating, and thin structures. The analysis focuses on a simplified model of these nebulae, which is based on a two-dimensional representation of the gas and its rotational velocity aligned in the same plane. The study considers the impact of gravity, magnetic forces, and ambipolar diffusion on the instability, which is characterized by a specific type of wave with a toroidal motion. The research reveals that ambipolar diffusion suppresses the instability, which is, however, counteracted by the presence of non-ideal magnetic effects. The instability is also influenced by the rotation of the nebula, which is more pronounced in low-rotating nebulae, while less so in those with high rotational velocities. The study's findings are relevant to the formation of filaments in star-forming regions.

The effects of repeated measurements on quantum systems have been thoroughly researched in the domain where the coupling strength is relatively low. This work investigates these effects under conditions of relatively strong coupling, where the typical time scales associated with measurement and system dynamics exhibit a substantial difference. Utilizing the quantum master equation for a two-level system interacting with a cavity field, we demonstrate that the Zeno and anti-Zeno phenomena can still be observed in the strong coupling regime, albeit with the coupling strength serving as the'measurement angle.' Our study reveals that the behavior of these phenomena is influenced by the ratio of the coupling strength to the energy gap, resulting in distinct dynamics for relatively strong coupling, even when this ratio is significantly higher than one.

This research examines the properties of a spin-1/2 Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions within a non-uniform external field. By utilizing the Holstein-Primakoff transformation and simplifying the model's interaction terms, we convert the Hamiltonian into a more manageable, analytically solvable quantum field theory. This framework enables us to calculate the self-energy of the order parameter and compute the corrections to its value at zero temperature. Our findings demonstrate that the corrections decrease in magnitude as the temperature rises, and we also derive the specific heat capacity of the system at various temperatures. Notably, the specific heat capacity exhibits a maximum at a temperature intermediate to the critical temperature, and its value at zero temperature aligns with established theoretical predictions.

The movement of a swarm of quadrotors from an initial configuration to a target configuration requires a set of feasible trajectories. Current methods, which rely on mixed-integer linear programming, pose difficulties as the number of quadrotors increases. To mitigate this limitation, we have developed a new approach that breaks down complex 3D planning problems into smaller, interconnected 1D problems. This decomposition, which is based on a linear model predictive control framework, allows for the use of pre-computed parameters. To the best of our knowledge, our method is the first to scale multi-quadrotor path planning to the level of hundreds without compromising efficiency or safety.

Unsupervised learning methods have gained popularity in robotics for adapting simulation models to real-world environments, but these models often fail when faced with diverse real-world scenarios. This paper presents CARLANE, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of unsupervised domain adaptation techniques in path detection tasks, utilizing simulated 3D point cloud data from the CARLA simulation software. The software provides a wide range of real-world environments captured through citizen contributions, allowing for the creation of 20 diverse domains with 100 unique scenarios for each domain. The proposed benchmark enables the assessment of generalization capabilities of unsupervised learning methods in path detection tasks, including the evaluation of current state-of-the-art techniques using a baseline approach. The results indicate that even the most advanced methods struggle to achieve optimal performance on unseen domains, highlighting the need for further research in this area. The CARLANE benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/alejandro-antonini/carlane.

Our research involves studying how nanoparticles affect the wettability of hydrogel contact points using 3D printing technology to create hydrogel-based models. We discovered that including these particles significantly boosts the contact angle, increasing it by more than double, to a value of approximately 60 degrees, even when the hydrogel alone has a very small contact angle. We also found that the contact angle follows a predictable logarithmic relationship to the amount of particles present, suggesting a way to control the contact angle by adjusting the amount of particles used.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to unprecedented changes in the way students learn, with widespread adoption of hybrid and fully online classes across education systems worldwide. Despite the rapid shift to online learning, research has yet to fully understand its impact on student engagement and academic performance. Building on existing studies that examined the effects of the COVID-19 era on student engagement and academic outcomes, this research extends our previous work by analyzing data from a massive online course offered by a top US public Ivy League university. The study employed a large-scale dataset of 1.1 million students who enrolled in the course between 2020 and 2021, with a focus on comparing their performance and engagement metrics with those of students from previous years. The results show that students learning online during the pandemic achieved comparable levels of academic performance while demonstrating lower levels of participation in discussions but higher participation in in-class discussions, despite spending less time on the course. These findings suggest that online learning during the pandemic may be more efficient but just as effective as in-person learning in terms of academic outcomes, with a potential need for further research to explore the trade-offs between learning efficiency and student engagement.

The Solar Wind's properties, such as its speed, density, and magnetic field strength, are crucial in understanding space weather. The Solar Wind's characteristics can be measured using various methods, including in-situ measurements and corona observations. The in-situ measurements provide accurate local readings, while coronal observations offer global and distant views. A new technique is developed to measure the Solar Wind's speed using the Swift wind scintillations and analyze it with an autoregressive model. The technique is validated by comparing its results with other, more accurate, methods, such as radio sounding and in-situ measurements. The technique is found to be reliable and can provide accurate readings, with a high level of agreement with other, more accurate, methods.

The open cluster UBC 274, which is in the process of disintegrating, has been under close observation from 2014 to 2019. By analyzing images from the Hubble Space Telescope, researchers have been able to track the movement of 23 stars within the cluster. Their findings show that the cluster's structure and the movement of stars can be accurately explained by a simulation that takes into account the cluster's rotation and the gravitational pull of the nearby Carina nebula. Furthermore, the study found that the cluster's stars are relatively old and the cluster itself is in the process of disintegrating. By analyzing the movement of the stars, the study found that the cluster's center of mass is moving at a speed of 0.8 plus or minus 0.1 millimeters per second. The study also found that the cluster's age is 0.5 million years and the metal content is 0.014 times that of the sun. The study suggests that the cluster's stars are likely to disperse in the next 10 to 20 million years, which will allow researchers to study the properties of the Carina nebula without the influence of the cluster's gravitational pull.

A single, high-quality sentence translation from a source to a target language is typically sufficient to enhance the quality of a low-quality parallel corpus. However, this method's effectiveness on sentence-level translations for improving corpus quality is not well established. This paper investigates the potential of using high-quality individual translations to refine a weak, parallel corpus. We examine both positive and negative examples of sentence translations applied to the entire corpus and explore alternative approaches, such as using diverse, machine-generated translations to mimic human translations for corpus enhancement. We also compare our methods to a state-of-the-art approach that directly generates artificial sentences to enhance corpus quality.

We explore the entanglement dynamics in a model quantum spin chain system that incorporates a time-varying, local dissipative process, referred to as dynamic dissipation. This investigation centers around understanding how the entanglement between the system's left and right halves changes over time, particularly under the influence of a protocol that gradually increases the dissipation intensity on the right half of the chain. We examine the long-term entanglement behavior in relation to the dissipation protocol's characteristics, identifying distinct entanglement regimes based on the dissipation's duration and strength. Our research reveals a transition from logarithmic entanglement growth to a saturation of entanglement entropy, ranging from a constant value to a linear decrease with increasing dissipation strength. Furthermore, we observe that the entanglement entropy's dependence on the dissipation duration is also multifaceted, resulting in a logarithmic increase, a saturation, or a decrease. We also explore the entanglement dynamics in relation to the system's temperature and the dissipation's influence on the environment, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex entanglement behavior of this quantum spin chain system.

The spin-orbit coupling in transition metal dichalcogenides has garnered significant attention due to its unique properties. In these materials, the spin-orbit splitting is influenced by the crystal structure, resulting in either a weak or moderate effect. The recent discovery of flat bands in transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures presents an opportunity to amplify the spin-orbit coupling. We have investigated the effects of crystal structure and heterostructure band topology on spin-orbit coupling and found that it can be controlled by adjusting the crystal structure and band filling, with the effective spin-orbit coupling varying by a factor of up to 100. This study sheds light on the spin-orbit coupling in transition metal dichalcogenides and provides insights for the design of novel electronic and spintronic devices.

A fundamental concept in information processing is the reservoir bit, a two-state system that facilitates energy transfer. We explore the characteristics of a single reservoir bit in various dimensions, specifically its ability to reach a thermal equilibrium when connected to a system with unlimited energy. Our research reveals that this equilibrium occurs when the system absorbs a certain threshold of energy, and we identify the conditions under which this happens. Notably, a system with limited energy levels can absorb more energy than one with more levels, and we also determine that, in the long run, the system-state matrix of a single reservoir bit in any dimension converges to a specific type of matrix.

The development of a compact, miniaturized version of the GaN
$\cdot$ Xe atom laser is underway, utilizing an unprocessed GaN-on-sapphire
substrate. To evaluate the suitability of this material, the surface topography and
atom-surface interaction potential of the untreated GaN-on-sapphire were studied.
Using atomic force microscopy, the roughness of the surface was found to be high, with
a root mean square of 16.2 nm, and a maximum amplitude of 20.6 nm. This is
significantly higher than that of a standard GaN single crystal wafer. This is
because GaN-on-surface material is typically grown using a layer-by-layer process. The
surface of the GaN-on-surface material was found to be more hydrophobic compared to a
standard GaN single crystal wafer. Additionally, the surface of the GaN-on-surface
material was found to be more resistant to adsorption, as evidenced by the lower
coverage of Xe atoms. This is likely due to the surface's higher energy state. Overall,
the results suggest that the GaN-on-surface material may not be suitable for the
miniaturized laser application.

This research project involves developing a Lagrange Finite Element Method implementation in a Lagrange-Maxwell system, utilizing the MFEM library. The solution method employs Lagrange tensor product polynomials of order three for electromagnetic field components. The associated Lagrange basis functions are derived by designating standard tensor product polynomials as reference basis functions, extending their respective supports to encompass the Lagrange interpolation degree in each spatial dimension. The study contrasts this method with the Mixed Finite Element Method, comparing it with the Nedelec edge-based formulation, specifically examining the M3FEM implementation in this context.

We investigate the evolution of a model featuring dark matter and dark energy that interact through a gravity-mediated mechanism, with a specific scenario in which a general form for the interaction term is considered. The evolution equations are solved using a numerical approach for a wide range of initial conditions, and the results are presented in a series of phase space diagrams. These diagrams reveal the existence of stable equilibrium points, and the model's behavior is further analyzed using the statefinder parameter in relation to the equation of state parameter. The findings indicate that the model aligns with current observations, and the statefinder parameter graph exhibits a characteristic feature associated with the quintessence scenario.

The radio bursts linked to TDEs share characteristics with shock-driven radio bursts from solar and stellar shocks, including narrow spectral bands and short durations. We propose that these bursts are generated by shocks driven by coronal mass ejections interacting with the interstellar medium. The proposed mechanism involves a shock-driven radio burst similar to those observed in stellar shocks, with the shock's normal vector oriented almost perpendicularly to the underlying magnetic field. The anisotropic radio propagation is consistent with observations of TDE bursts, and the perpendicular orientation is typical of the magnetic field in the interstellar medium. The perpendicular shock-driven radio bursts exhibit a characteristic frequency drift, with the lower-frequency radiation emitted first. The combination of the shock's normal vector orientation and the magnetic field direction in the interstellar medium enables the efficient conversion of the shock's kinetic energy into electromagnetic energy.

A mathematical model of the acoustic interaction with a micro-bubble attached to a stiff wall has been developed using the Keller-Ochmann boundary integral formulation at the bubble-wall interface. The model considers the bubble's non-linear resonance behavior in response to varying acoustic wave amplitudes and frequencies. Computational results indicate a significant increase in bubble response at amplitudes exceeding 1 volt per meter and frequencies within the bubble's fundamental resonant frequency. Theoretical calculations show that the acoustic energy required to generate a stable micro-bubble is significantly lower than that needed to create a void in water, resulting in a lower energy threshold for bubble formation. The model also predicts that the acoustic driving force required to sustain a stable micro-bubble is minimal, approaching zero, and that the bubble's oscillation frequency is comparable to that of a void.

In our research, we introduce MUSER, a dataset consisting of high-definition videos featuring real human subjects engaging in a handgrip strength test under varying levels of stress. We incorporate a supplementary task to investigate the role of emotional awareness in recognizing physical tension. MUSER is the first publicly accessible dataset of its kind, utilizing high-definition video, to assess tension recognition in human subjects over time. We also introduce a novel metric to evaluate the temporal quality of our dataset. MUSER is accessible at https://github.com/usc-aithi/muser

We introduce PanGEA, an environment simulation framework that enables the
development of agents capable of solving complex tasks in large-scale, realistic
scenarios. This comprehensive toolkit facilitates flexible task creation, agent
training, single-agent or multi-agent evaluation, and in-depth analysis of
adversarial behavior. Built using Python and PyTorch, PanGEA is designed to be
modular, allowing users to create and customize their own tasks and environments
using a user-friendly command-line interface. By showcasing PanGEA through
illustrative examples, we highlight its features and utility in a range of
applications.

We have developed a new model to explain how massive elliptical galaxies acquire their stars. This model takes into account the effects of star formation occurring in groups of stars that vary in metal content, and groups these stars into 'populations' based on their metal content. We have found that the rate at which stars form in elliptical galaxies is typically slower than previously thought, and that the age of these galaxies is influenced by the time it takes for their stellar populations to form. We have also found that the gravitational potential of these galaxies is crucial in determining the age of their stellar populations, and that galaxies that are more massive tend to have older populations. A new approach to image compressive sensing reconstruction is proposed, which incorporates the collective l1-norm and collective sparse representation into a non-linear model, and is demonstrated to outperform current methods using both real-world and synthetic data.

Deep learning models have been successful in facial skin lesion detection tasks, 
yet they often struggle with identifying specific skin issues due to their 
generalized approach. To overcome this limitation, we introduce RethNet, a 
segmentation network designed to classify individual skin lesions into one of 
several skin issue categories. Our proposed network consists of two distinct 
sub-networks that work in tandem to refine the general features extracted from 
the input image. The first sub-network uses recurrent neural networks to assign 
initial category labels to each skin lesion, while the second network refines 
these labels through a process of mutual learning. This innovative approach 
enables RethNet to learn and improve its performance on an item-by-item basis, 
resulting in superior performance on a variety of skin issue identification 
tasks.

This paper examines the efficiency and computational complexity of decoding sequential messages encoded with high-density, low-noise distortion PAC codes under a specific channel condition. Under this condition, it's established that sequential decoding produces a substantial number of necessary calculations, specifically growing at an exponential rate with code length and approaching the maximum possible complexity of solving NP-complete problems. Consequently, this implies that sequential decoding is unlikely to be efficiently managed by current computing systems for extended code lengths.

Online learning platforms have gained popularity, but face difficulties in
engaging users who are new to online learning, known as "cold-start" users. 
These users often lack the necessary skills and confidence to begin a course.
To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach that combines the 
transitional learning method with sequential recommendations to encourage
new users to start their online journey. Our proposed framework, which is
based on Markov Decision Process (MDP), aims to maximize the users' learning
effectiveness and overall satisfaction. Through sequential recommendations,
we guide users to select the most suitable courses for their skill levels and
objectives, while the transitional learning phase helps bridge existing gaps
in their knowledge. Experimental results on real-world data demonstrate the
success of our approach, achieving a significant improvement in course
enrollment rates for users who were previously unable to access online
education.

Galactic ultrahigh energy cosmic rays are composed primarily of protons and nuclei, with energies exceeding 40 EeV, produced through the acceleration of supersonic shocks within molecular clouds and in the vicinity of stellar winds. These cosmic rays may be generated by supernovae, stellar wind interactions, and cloud collisions, with an understanding still emerging as to the dominant source responsible for their origin. The galactic radiation fields and magnetic fields play a crucial role in determining the cosmic ray composition and energy levels through photo-disintegration and acceleration processes. The cosmic ray flux and energy levels are also significantly affected by the interstellar medium and self-gravity of cosmic ray particles, as well as particle acceleration and escape mechanisms. This review provides an overview of the current understanding of the cosmic ray properties and their interactions within the galaxy.

The Planetary Defense and Exploration (DART) mission, set for launch in 2025, will employ an impactor with a specific shape and speed to collide with the asteroid DART, a small, near-Earth object, that demonstrates a specific internal structure and ideal response to the impact. The impactor's shape is designed to ensure the asteroid's center of mass remains unchanged before and after the impact. Researchers have developed a new analytical model to predict the momentum transfer resulting from an impact with an arbitrary projectile. The new model was validated through comparisons with numerical simulations of various impacts with different shapes and materials. The results indicate that the momentum transfer is influenced by factors such as the impactor's shape, size, and material properties, as well as the target's porosity. The new model was then applied to several scenarios, including impacts with different materials and shapes, to demonstrate its accuracy. The research also considered the effects of spin and non-spherical mass distributions on the momentum transfer. The new analytical model was found to be reliable and efficient, making it a valuable tool for the DART mission.

In autonomous driving, through-the-windshield (TWW) operators pose a significant threat to driverless vehicles. These individuals, often homeless and on the lookout for handouts, may approach vehicles in the name of hitchhiking, panhandling, or vandalism. Existing TWW detection systems have limitations, including those that utilize cameras, which are vulnerable to occlusions, and LIDAR systems, which are expensive and require precise calibration. This research presents a novel, low-cost, and real-time TWW detection system that combines multiple sensors to enhance detection accuracy. A fusion algorithm is employed to integrate data from each sensor, and a neural network classifier is used to identify TWW individuals. This approach leverages the strengths of each sensor, and a supporting system is proposed to facilitate real-time TAWW detection in vehicles.

This study delves into the role of extensive text descriptions, known as blurbs, within the context of programming language repositories. While repositories are essential for disseminating open-source software, little consideration is given to the design principles that facilitate effective knowledge transfer between developers. By analyzing a dataset consisting of 24,000 Bluhtext blurbs, this research uncovers key design elements that contribute to a better understanding of programming languages. Results indicate that blurbs effectively convey the end result of a programming language, often represented by a specific function. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of clarity, consistency, and accuracy in blurbs through the development of design principles. The findings suggest that researchers and developers can utilize Bluhtext to enhance their understanding of programming languages, thereby creating a valuable resource for the software engineering community.

Causal inference using observational data is often hindered by missing covariates, 
and time-series data often results in censored outcomes. This combination 
presents significant challenges for learning about unobserved confounders and 
censored data. We introduce a novel approach, the multistage estimator, 
comprised of an initial stage utilizing supervised learning to estimate missing 
covariates and a subsequent stage estimating causal effects using the 
propensity score stratification method. We also propose a two-stage estimator 
that incorporates outcome regression, and derive its asymptotic properties. 
The proposed methods are demonstrated on real-world and synthetic data, 
demonstrating their effectiveness.

A widely-held conjecture about the complete elliptic integral of the first kind has been verified by our research. We prove that for specific, nearly equivalent forms of the conjecture, the function $f(a)$ is concave, and its first and second derivatives satisfy certain relationships. Notably, our findings confirm a crucial hypothesis from a recent study, and we provide an alternative, simpler proof compared to the original method.

A novel inductive method for learning agents has been developed, focusing on
dissecting the learning process into two stages: initial parameter estimation and
target-oriented fine-tuning. This two-part approach enables the agent to learn
from sparse expert data by first approximating optimal parameters, and then adjust
its policy towards matching expert behavior as a second step. By leveraging this
decomposed method, agents can efficiently replicate expert strategies using
minimal demonstration information, resulting in the following benefits:
(1) Reduced demonstration data requirements; (2) Improved expert policy
replication; (3) Enhanced sample efficiency; (4) Simplified and more
efficient learning processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method
by applying it to various domains such as gridworlds, StarCraft, and even human
behavior, showcasing its potential to efficiently reproduce expert strategies in
complex domains with limited demonstration data.

The rapid advancement of the web has significantly increased the speed of information dissemination, yet it also facilitated the spread of manipulated data, such as altered and fake news. Given the scarcity of research addressing fake news in the Arab world, this study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of its various types and proposes innovative datasets along with an identification model tailored for Arabic altered and fake news. To develop these datasets, this research utilizes a multi-step approach that integrates both automated data creation and manual labeling processes. The study then proposes a cutting-edge model that integrates both text and image features, leveraging multiple deep learning architectures, to identify Arabic altered and fake news. The performance of the developed model is evaluated using two datasets, and the results indicate that it achieves impressive performance on the created test dataset, boasting an F1-score of 0.999.

The article in question, "Torsion groups of rational elliptic curves over the compositum of all $D_4$ extensions of the rational fields," originally published in the "Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society" volume 116, issue 2, in 2018, requires a correction due to an error found in the final section, "Further discussion." This mistake concerns the divisibility of the order of the torsion subgroup of rational elliptic curves in specific extensions, leading to an error that needs to be addressed.

We investigate the influence of noise on complex quantum systems consisting of multiple interacting qubits. We utilize the matrix product operator (MPO) method to accurately simulate noisy quantum systems. We demonstrate the MPO method's ability to capture both local and non-local correlations in many-body quantum systems. We also show that the MPO representation of a noisy quantum channel can be derived from the unitary equivalent Hamiltonian of the channel. We apply the MPO method to a specific model of noise, the depolarizing channel, and find that the method's results are in agreement with alternative theoretical methods. We also discuss the MPO method's efficiency and limitations in simulating noisy quantum systems.

We introduce a novel, data-driven approach to targeted web scraping, which focuses on specific user groups by leveraging their interaction patterns with websites. This approach combines the advantages of both rule-based and machine learning-based methods to efficiently navigate and crawl web pages. A hierarchical model is created to simulate the user behavior, consisting of a decision tree that selects the next hyperparameters (e.g. browser, device, user agent) and a queue of queued scraping models that handle data collection. The model parameters are learned through a reinforcement learning algorithm that maximizes the return based on the collected data. This approach is validated by comparing the crawling efficiency of simulated user models with actual user behavior on multiple websites. The results show that our simulated models outperform rules-based models in terms of resource utilization and data collection efficiency.

Our research focuses on a specific type of event information centered around objects,
examining how the same real-world incident can be represented in distinct ways.
We've created a framework consisting of three categories: entity-based, attribute-based,
and interaction-based events, which allow for varied interpretations of the same occurrence.
We've also developed a comprehensive dataset featuring 1,000 annotated instances and 2,000
associated variations, showcasing different event perspectives and descriptions. Furthermore,
we've designed a series of automated tasks to replicate the process of finding equivalent
event variations, achieve high accuracy using pre-trained models, and establish a baseline
for future work on this task. Our annotated dataset and accompanying resources are available
at https://www.mpi-inf.mpg.de/events/2022/evendat/.

A novel method of wavefield restoration has been developed to mitigate the effects of high-frequency noise in image gathers by combining total least squares and weighted matrix decomposition. This approach is effective for large-scale 2D and 3D problems, where the size of the coefficient matrix can be enormous, and each individual row can represent a seismic source location. To tackle this issue, we employ limited-subspace techniques that approximate the coefficient matrix using a low-dimensional space. This enables us to solve a series of smaller problems, and we have developed a method to solve the overall problem by solving each problem once and efficiently combining the solutions. This approach is more efficient than other decomposition methods and requires less computational work than traditional methods like total least squares. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the new method outperforms total least squares and weighted matrix decompositions in terms of both numerical accuracy and computational time.

A flat and wide-angle optical system is highly sought after for its potential to revolutionize optical technology, but designing such a system is complex due to the need for precise control over the optical properties at every point. In this research, we introduce a comprehensive study on the characteristics of ultra-widefield-of-view metalenses made of nonlinear materials, specifically quadratic nonlinear media. Theoretical analysis reveals that the refractive indices in the x and y planes must be identical to achieve a wide field of view, and numerical modeling enables the design of metalenses with a 60-degree viewing area. Theoretical and experimental results show that the metalenses can focus light within its 30-degree numerical aperture, and the field of view can be expanded by incorporating a prism to redirect light, achieving a 120-degree viewing area.

A novel plasma device has been developed that utilizes high-velocity plasma streams produced by radio-frequency-driven atmospheric pressure plasma to study the interplay between plasma and neutral gases. The neutral gas density and temperature are monitored and found to be influenced by plasma boundary shifts caused by RF excitation, which in turn affects the plasma propagation velocity. A two-temperature model is used to simulate the plasma-neutral gas interactions, with the inclusion of drag forces and heating to accurately describe the plasma motion. The model is compared with experimental results and shows a strong correlation, with the simulations successfully predicting the plasma and neutral gas behavior.

Einstein's gravity theory, when combined with a power-law potential, accurately models the behavior of black strings and black rings across all dimensions. When a specific type of string correction is applied, it leads to the formation of silhouettes around these black objects, resulting from gravitational lensing effects. This study examines how the frequency of massive particles and quasinormal modes are affected by this type of string correction in higher-dimensional black objects, and shows that the correction influences the observed silhouette.

Pulsar timing arrays aim to detect stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds through cross-correlating signal data, but an alternative method has been proposed using common-band filtering on pulsar timing data, which is mathematically equivalent to the established cross-correlation technique, when considering all pulsars. However, due to the discrete nature of pulsar data, a common filtering approach is impractical, instead a modified method using a red time-domain pulsar times series is proposed, which is mathematically equivalent to the cross-correlation method, and is capable of producing the same results, with the added benefit of being more efficient for red noise pulsars.

Highly regular, separable, and efficient LDPC codes known as QRAC codes are highly sought after for various applications, and they exhibit unique properties. These codes have a unique structure that can be represented by a particular type of matrix known as a generator matrix, which is constrained within a certain space. This paper proposes a new criterion for identifying QRAC codes, which is based on the minimum distance between any two non-parallel check equations in a particular set of equations. This criterion is more stringent than previous methods and can be used to generate a large number of QRAC codes with specific properties. The proposed method has been implemented and has shown its effectiveness in identifying QRAC codes, which are highly efficient for certain types of channel models.

We establish a class of truncated Toeplitz operators using matrix-valued kernels that are derived from unbounded functions on the unit circle with limited growth. These operators can be related to those generated by bounded functions through a transformation that preserves key characteristics, such as parabolicity for kernels and the commutant of the system for the associated TOTs. This equivalence post extension maintains the essential properties of the operators, including parabolicity for the kernels and the commutant of the system for the TOTs.

In a Bayesian framework, the influence of new data on an existing model or hypothesis is assessed through the posterior influence coefficient. This value can be derived from the relationship between an updated posterior distribution and the initial prior distribution following a statistical test. The influence coefficient is analogous to a standardized regression coefficient in the context of the Bayesian posterior mean. For sequential statistical tests, this influence is calculated based on multinomial probabilities, which allow for a closed-form solution. The influence coefficient is found to be a function of the initial posterior distribution, the number of trials, and the observed outcome. This value can be used to determine the expected influence of new data, which is found to decrease as the number of trials increases. The influence coefficient is also used to determine the Bayesian equivalent of the p-value, which is the Bayesian influence coefficient. This value is found to be a function of the initial posterior distribution, the number of trials, and the observed outcome. The Bayesian influence coefficient is used to determine the posterior probability that the null hypothesis is false, which is found to be equivalent to 1 minus the influence coefficient. The influence coefficient is also found to be a function of the Bayesian posterior probability that the null hypothesis is false, which is used to determine the Bayesian equivalent of the p-value.

In situations where an audio system's training and operational environments differ significantly, the audio data's distribution can be severely impacted, often resulting in unexpected behavior. In this paper, we investigate an unsupervised approach to address this domain shift issue by utilizing unsupervised learning and visualizing high-dimensional audio features using dimensionality reduction techniques. Our proposed method, which combines the capabilities of UMAP and spectrogram-based feature extraction, aims to identify anomalous audio signals. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively detects unusual audio signals in real-time, while minimizing false positives and negatives.

In the context of SU(N) fermions at low densities and near the superfluid transition, we find that the ground state exhibits a disordered, ferromagnetic trait that's linked to the balance between long-range and short-range correlations, and persists even when N is large. We also identify a disordered phase characterized by the presence of a 'nomadic' order parameter that changes randomly with any given axis rotation, and speculate about its potential at larger N values.

This study examines the potential of using stacking analysis to enhance the
sensitivity of gamma-ray pulsars to previously undetected signals. By combining
the pulsar candidates from the third Fermi-LAT source catalog, the analysis
investigates pulsar rotation periods and distances. Our results indicate that
a stacking analysis can yield more sensitive outcomes than individual source
analyses for certain pulsars. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a distinct
relationship between gamma-ray flux and pulsar luminosity for the analyzed
sample. Additionally, the study explores the influence of various parameters
on the sensitivity of the analysis, such as the candidate selection method,
the pulsar candidate distribution, and the analysis field of view.

In this research, a theoretical model is developed to describe the low-energy excitations within a fractional quantum Hall system, which incorporates a specific property. The study reveals that the energy spectrum of these excitations exhibits a specific arrangement, with the effect of a certain type of energy level becoming less pronounced as this property increases in magnitude. The analysis also shows that the energy levels exhibit a certain type of energy correlation, which can be used to derive a set of rules governing the energy levels. The results of this analysis indicate that the energy levels exhibit a significant amount of variation in their behavior as the density of the system changes. The effect of adding a magnetic field on the energy levels is also examined, which results in the emergence of a specific type of energy level. The study provides a set of rules governing the energy levels, which can be used to describe the low-energy behavior of this system.

The Intense Energy Occurrences experiment, utilizing the High Intensity and AcCELERATOR Interactions research racking (HIADIAI) facility, incorporates a modified RLC resonant circuit to produce intense radio-frequency fields, reaching up to 50 MV/m. This setup enables the creation of intense energy occurrences in vacuum, plasma, and dielectric materials, with the current focus on the latter two. We have tested the setup on three 3D-printed ceramic samples, observing a notable enhancement in the occurrence intensity due to the material's high dielectric constant. Additionally, we have employed the experiment to analyze the breakdown threshold of vacuum, which is influenced by the resonant frequency, the length of the circuit's tuned section, and the applied radio-frequency power.

The existence of smooth solutions to the truncated Boltzmann equation is demonstrated under the condition that the maximum possible collision frequency is below a specific value. This result holds even when the initial conditions are known only to a low level of detail.

Machine learning models are typically trained using a supervised approach, 
relying on accurate labels to generate optimal predictions. However, due to 
various limitations, these labels often contain errors, compromising model 
performance. To mitigate this issue, our research focuses on developing 
classifiers that remain reliable even when faced with intentionally flawed data, 
as is the case with adversarial attacks. By utilizing a straightforward yet 
effective method, we can effectively counterbalance the impact of such errors, 
resulting in improved classification outcomes despite the presence of corrupted 
labels.

In the case of a fixed even subset S of the 24-element set Gamma, consisting of the 12 antipodal pairs of elements in Gamma along with 6 additional elements, a code is formed by the orbits of the subgroup of order 4 produced by the group Gamma with S as a defining set. We identify the automorphism groups, determine the number of orbits under different automorphism groups, and classify the possible symmetries for the resulting code when S is a proper non-empty subset of Gamma, with specific considerations given for the possible configurations when S is empty or entire Gamma.

A binary star system within the open cluster M67, observed in the K2 dataset, features a primary star in its near end of main sequence life and a low-mass companion. By utilizing the cluster's known age and using Gaia's parallax measurements, the binary system's mass and orbital properties can be precisely determined. A study utilizing the K2 dataset has discovered a binary star system within the open cluster M67, comprising a near end of main sequence primary star and a low-mass companion. By leveraging the known age and parallax of the cluster, the binary system's mass and orbital properties can be calculated. A key finding of the study involves the accurate determination of the primary star's mass, which can be compared to theoretical models to assess their accuracy. A comparison of the binary system's properties to those of similar binary star systems observed in globular clusters indicates that the orbital properties of the binary system are consistent with those of other clusters of similar age and metallicity.

We are examining the well-known Schrödinger operator $L_c = -d^2/dx^2+cx^\alpha$ and focus on the equation $\mathscr{L}_c W = 0$, which has multiple solutions across various parameters $c$ and $x$. This equation has an infinite number of solutions when $0<\alpha<4$, and we are particularly interested in the non-trivial, positive, and strictly convex solutions. We aim to establish a sufficiency theorem for these solutions, and our approach is based on the fundamental solution $E_c(x)$ of the equation $\mathscr{L}_c W = 0$. This theorem is derived from the properties of $E_c(x)$, and we are considering the asymptotic behavior of $E_c(x)$ for large $x$.

A novel SPH method is proposed that conserves mass, momentum, and energy, and is particularly suited for simulating complex fluid interactions and transport phenomena. By leveraging a modified gradient estimation approach, the method achieves substantial reductions in force and divergence calculations of up to 80% and 90% respectively, while maintaining exceptional accuracy and smoothness. The proposed method is rigorously validated through a series of benchmark tests that demonstrate its efficacy in modeling diverse fluid dynamics, from simple shock interactions to complex astrophysical scenarios.

The primary objective of spectral super-enhancement is to extract a full spectrum from a single color image and for this purpose, a novel approach called the Spectral Super-Enhancement Network (SSEN) has been proposed. This new framework is based on the idea of a multi-level, multi-scale, and multi-path learning mechanism. This approach is divided into two main components: the first one is responsible for estimating the spectral intensity, and the second one is a functional module used to estimate the spectral intensity and its corresponding spectral density. In the era of big data, structuring and locating digital images effectively is a significant challenge. To address this, we have developed an innovative, context-aware system for automatically assigning geographical locations and relevant attributes to images. Using a combination of crowdsourced data, maps, and location-specific guidelines, our system identifies the spatial coordinates and context of an image by analyzing its content. To improve the accuracy of this process, we have created a novel, context-dependent framework that utilizes a deep neural network to select the most relevant geotags and contexts from a predefined knowledge base. These context-aware parameters enable the system to focus on features that are crucial for making a correct geotagging decision, thus reducing the risk of incorrect assignments. To evaluate the performance of our approach, we have conducted experiments using real-world images and compared the results with a standard deep learning method. The evaluation revealed that our proposed method achieves superior accuracy, with an increase of 6.2% in average precision compared to the baseline.

The removal of dams across international dam systems is being pursued as a means to restore ecosystems and mitigate the negative impacts of hydroelectric power on communities. A significant challenge in the dam removal process is accurately measuring the remaining storage levels through remote observations. This study presents a novel approach to address this issue by leveraging a deep learning model that can be trained using customized metrics. The proposed method outperformed existing benchmark techniques in a comprehensive evaluation across 12 test datasets. Furthermore, our technique enables the creation of a dam removal storage level inference model from publicly available satellite imagery, without requiring prior information about the dam's geometry or the pre-flood storage capacity. The developed model can be used to estimate the storage levels of dams across the globe, facilitating a more accurate assessment of dam removal impacts on surrounding communities.

A Quantized Finite Size (QFS) zone is a region within a crystal where the electronic density of states is restricted due to the experimental constraints of both size and resolution, where the size refers to the available space for electron distribution and resolution pertains to the achievable accuracy in measuring the density of electronic states.

E-commerce and retail businesses utilize product categorization to streamline operations, but it's a complex task due to numerous possible categories and a large number of products to categorize. To improve the accuracy of point-of-attractance category forecasting, we've developed a method that combines text and visual data in a transformer-based framework. Our approach outperforms existing methods when solely relying on text or visuals, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating both modalities.

The primary objective of corporate management is to maximize shareholder value, which has become increasingly complex with the emergence of large-scale institutional investors and sophisticated financial products. Consequently, analyzing the dynamics of share price fluctuations is a significant challenge. This study focuses on the impact of earnings calls on share price movements, specifically examining the impact of question types on subsequent share price developments. Through a detailed annotation process, the study presents a publicly available dataset of 500 questions from 26 conference calls, providing valuable insights for quantitative analysts in the finance industry.

The placement of sensors in a network can be crucial to a specific application, and several approaches have been developed to optimize sensor placement based on predetermined criteria. However, these methods typically rely on a uniform communication radius, which may not be applicable to all scenarios. In this study, we investigate the problem of sensor placement in a 2D space, focusing on uniform and diverse networks with variable node densities. We introduce a novel measure to evaluate sensor density distribution and propose a flexible placement strategy that accommodates different communication radii. This strategy includes a node selection algorithm and a random sensor placement algorithm, which can be combined to optimize sensor density distribution. We also present a simulation-based approach to accelerate the optimization process, and our findings indicate that this method can effectively improve sensor density distribution and diversity.

A novel quantum eigenstate selection method has been devised for finding the $k^{th}$ principal component of a symmetric, positive-definite matrix $A$. This method, which utilizes polynomials and is based on previous work by Harrow, Iyer, and Trevisan, can be applied to a wide range of problems, including solving systems of linear equations. It has been shown that this method can be used to solve a generalized quantum linear system in a single query, and its potential has been applied to a variety of real-world applications, including matrix inversion, eigenanalysis, and low rank matrix approximation.

We investigate the interaction of topological defects within a nonlinear medium 
under the influence of an external magnetic field. The theoretical framework is based 
on the infant skyrmion model, and numerical methods are employed to demonstrate 
the formation of compactly sized gauge fields. Specifically, we examine the role 
of nonlinearity in stabilizing these compact gauge fields and show that they can 
emerge in a medium at rest, even without an initial defect, due to the external 
magnetic field.

Investigations into novel physics phenomena, specifically those beyond the Standard Model, are conducted using a theoretical framework known as the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). By incorporating dimension-6 operators, this framework enables the exploration of a wide range of possible scenarios, including those involving new particles and forces. The primary objective of these investigations is to set a limit on the strength of these new interactions or to uncover potential signs of their presence. In this study, we examine the discovery potential of these dimension-6 operators at current and forthcoming particle accelerator facilities, with a particular emphasis on their implications for the Higgs, electroweak, and top sectors.

A diamond mechanical resonator with a ferromagnetic tip, attached to a commercial gyroscope, was utilized in a experiment to investigate the effect of nuclear spin on its resonance. The device was then exposed to a weak magnetic field of approximately 5 millitesla as it vibrated at a frequency of 2.5 kilohertz, revealing a distinct change in its response of about 0.2--0.3 nanotesla per tesla per second squared upon a magnetic field change every ten seconds. Notably, the observed responses were found to be either positive or negative, suggesting that the magnetic anisotropy of the diamond's nitrogen vacancy centers is negligible. The experiment's findings align with theoretical predictions, indicating that the observed magnetic sensitivity arises from the interaction between the diamond's nuclear spins and the applied magnetic field through the spin-to-orbital angular momentum transfer from the ferromagnetic tip.

The development of whole-cell models is a complex task driven by the need to understand the intricate interactions within living cells. Recent advances in experimental data analysis, simulation methods, and mathematical modeling have created a foundation for constructing whole-cell models. This review provides an overview of the latest progress in whole-cell simulation, focusing on key components such as signal flow, models, and simulations, as well as the challenges involved in creating whole-cell models.

This paper investigates the challenge of locating a target object with multiple viewpoints using a mobile camera. The problem is complicated by changing object perspectives, environmental factors, and camera movements, affecting image quality and distortion. To address this, we propose a novel mobile multi-view object visual search system capable of retrieving the target object from a set of real-time query images, regardless of the target's orientation or location. The system first identifies the target's location in each query image using a multi-scale feature matching approach and then aggregates the resulting features to obtain a comprehensive representation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately retrieving the target object from multiple viewpoints and its robustness to various environmental factors.

Hyperdimensional (HD) computing is a promising new field that has the
potential to outperform traditional machine learning methods in various tasks.
In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of two advanced HD tactics,
namely, utilizing both linear and non-linear codes as input features, and developing
a multi-stage classification system. By employing these techniques, we have achieved
a higher F1 score of 0.78 on the linear code HD method and 0.83 on the non-linear
code HD method when classifying seizure data from the scalp, exceeding the
performance of our initial HD method and comparable results obtained with
traditional classification algorithms.

Future observations of gravitational waves from compact binary systems will enable researchers to study the distant universe in various ways. This will involve using a specific method called standard siren cosmology, which can provide insights into the universe's expansion rate, particularly through two types of measurements. One of these is based on the distance modulus, which calculates the distance to distant sources, while the other is derived from the distance-dependent gravitational wave signal. This study focuses on the distance modulus measurement, calculating the distance to binary black holes based on their signal strength and detection instruments. By using the distance to these sources, we can constrain the universe's expansion rate, and our results show that the distance to binary black holes detected by future deci-hertz instruments will be precise enough to provide a relatively small but significant constraint on the universe's expansion rate, particularly for low redshift sources.

This study presents an extension to the existing QALD-9 dataset, consisting of 9,406 questions in 7 languages and 2 source databases, accompanied by relevant answers and database identifiers. The new iteration, named QALD-9-plus, incorporates 2,716 new questions and expands the number of languages to 10, thereby enhancing multilinguality. The QALD-9 dataset has been instrumental in facilitating research in question answering, and its impact can be seen in the development of open-domain QA systems. The QALD-9 dataset has been particularly influential in supporting multilingual QA research, and its QALD-9-plus iteration further broadens its linguistic scope. The QALD-9-plus corpus was compiled by recruiting native speakers who were tasked with formulating responses to given questions in their native languages, thereby ensuring that both question-answer pairs and answers are accurately annotated and, in the case of answers, linguistically and semantically precise.

The machine learning community has been actively exploring various techniques to enhance the interpretability of models. This involves utilizing techniques such as resampling and renaming machine learning features to gain a deeper understanding of their internal workings. However, these methods often struggle to provide a clear and concise summary of their findings. This paper introduces a new approach called the executive function framework, which aims to address this issue by efficiently aggregating insights from resampling and renaming models. Our method utilizes a simulated annealing technique to optimize a posteriori summary sets, which satisfy a predefined set of criteria. This involves minimizing the number of summary features while maximizing their predictive power and variance. Our results demonstrate that this approach can effectively identify a smaller set of more informative features, even when compared to alternative methods. This is evident from our experiments on real-world datasets.

As medical imaging datasets are becoming increasingly accessible, there's a pressing need for content-based retrieval systems that can effectively locate similar images. However, medical image databases contain biased information embedded within both the images and the metadata, which can skew content-based retrieval outcomes. Research has shown that medical image metadata often reflects societal biases. To address these issues, we've developed a framework that leverages intrinsic prejudice detection to identify and mitigate bias in medical image collections. Our method involves quantifying prejudice using a single image, and we've created a novel metric to assess its presence. We've also developed a method to effectively remove prejudice from a single image, and we've demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing prejudice in downstream applications through extensive experiments across various datasets.

Metric learning has advanced significantly due to the incorporation of various losses, yet these losses are often hindered by noisy labels. To address this issue, researchers have proposed proxy-labels for noisy data, but existing methods lack sufficient supervision to accurately generate these labels. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel loss function called Sleek Proxy-Anchor Loss (SPAL), which utilizes proxy-labels in conjunction with query-anchor pairs to train networks effectively. SPAL is comprised of two essential components: a proxy-label generator and a metric loss function, both of which are designed to work in tandem to improve performance. The loss function, SPAL, is constructed by combining the proxy-labels with the standard triplet loss function, which is then optimized through end-to-end training. Experimental results demonstrate that SPAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in noisy data scenarios, and when used in conjunction with clean labels, the network achieves superior results, surpassing those obtained by base models trained with clean labels.

The $P_{gg}$, the correlation function of the density gradient, holds significant potential for understanding the cosmological limitations imposed by non-Gaussianity. This function, previously identified as the primary source of cosmic variance in N-body simulations, is a comprehensive measure of non-Gaussianity in the density field. In this study, we calculate the $P_{gg}$ for various redshift surveys and compare it to the conventional $P_{gg}$, which is a comprehensive measure of non-Gaussianity in the density field. We also investigate the impact of redshift survey boundaries on the $P_{gg}$ and propose an innovative approach to estimate the $P_{gg}$ using the power spectrum of the density field.

A theoretical model of a d-wave topological superconductor has been created, which extends beyond the conventional SO(3) symmetry governing spin and pairing degrees of freedom, incorporating the additional component of spin-orbit coupling that leads to SO(5) symmetry. This framework enables a unified quantum field theory to describe both the normal and superconducting states of the system. A key aspect of this model is the identification of a single fermion field that remains invariant under all symmetries, facilitating the derivation of a comprehensive boson-fermion action that encompasses both the normal and superconducting phases. This theoretical framework provides a unified approach to studying topological superconductivity, offering a versatile platform for exploring its properties.

Researchers have successfully implemented and tested multiple avalanche detectors with the category MAPD (Metalized Avalanche Proportional Detector), which includes the original MAPD and its variants, MAPD-T (Thick), MAPD-L (Large Area), MAPD-Scint) with scintillation layer, MAPD-PM (Photo-MAPD) with a photo cathode and scintillators. The detectors employ a standard structure with a metalized anode and no additional electrodes. The detectors' characteristics are presented in this paper, including a discussion of their fabrication process and operating methods. The detectors' performance is compared with that of conventional PDs using solid anode electrodes. The results show that MAPD detectors have a lower operating voltage, increased sensitivity, and improved spatial resolution. The detectors' sensitivity is enhanced by employing an avalanche signal processing technique, which involves amplifying the avalanche current with a high gain. The detectors' gain is further increased by adding a scintillation layer, which leads to higher sensitivity. The detectors' spatial resolution is improved by introducing a photo-cathode with a micro-channel plate. The detectors' functionality is demonstrated by measuring the characteristics of X-ray pulses and detecting cosmic rays.

This article presents the primary genera of standard graded Cohen-Macaulay algebras, utilizing their Gorenstein standard bases and associated standard graded quotients. We demonstrate that the primary genera of such bases are invariant under standard graded equivalence, and explore connections between these genera and standard bases with a particular property known as being "Blinov. The paper also introduces an algorithm for determining the primary genera of standard graded algebras, and provides examples of standard graded equivalence classes that exhibit non-isomorphic primary genera.

A new, high-pressure investigation of the Aurivillius compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) has been conducted, focusing on the phase transitions it undergoes under high pressure. BFTO exhibits a complex structure consisting of four perovskite layers and two tetragonal layers of BiO. Initially, in this study, the phase behavior of BFTO under high pressure was studied using nuclear forward scattering, a non-destructive technique that provides information on the compound's structure. Our findings indicate that BFTO's phase remains unchanged up to 2.5 GPa, but above this threshold, it undergoes a phase transition. Subsequently, the phase remains stable under pressures up to 7 GPa. BFTO's magnetic properties were also examined at room pressure, and the results showed that the compound's magnetic behavior undergoes a significant transformation at 7 K. This critical temperature is found to decrease with increasing pressure, dropping from 7 K at 1GPa to 5 K at 7 GPa. Our investigation also revealed that the compound's magnetic properties can be described by a Brillouin-like curve, and the magnetic critical exponent is found to be 0.5, indicative of a second-order phase transition.

A new statistical method has been developed to evaluate and compare the costs incurred by trading, including a detailed description of a hypothetical case study. This analysis method, referred to as Bayesian Trading Expense Evaluation, leverages a Bayesian framework to calculate the combined trading expenses for multiple assets. By simulating asset prices, the BTXE uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to determine the parameters that best fit the data, allowing it to account for any level of correlation between assets. Through this approach, the method generates a ranking of brokers' algorithms based on their performance in a specific trading environment.

In the realm of integrated photonics, optomechanical devices have become a significant component, enabling a range of applications such as tunable filters and sensitive sensors. However, the development of completely adjustable devices has been hindered by the limitations of optomechanical interactions. This work presents a novel optomechanical add-drop design that leverages the unique properties of a specially configured resonator to enable independent tuning of add and drop ports. This device can be fabricated using established CMOS technology and has the potential to significantly expand the capabilities of integrated photonics by facilitating the creation of adaptable devices that can be seamlessly integrated within advanced photonic systems.

The internet has become an essential resource for creating and disseminating information on health and hygiene practices, with a vast amount of online content available. As many people rely on search engines and social media platforms to find information on health and hygiene, it is crucial to evaluate the accuracy and effectiveness of online health-related content to prevent the spread of diseases. This research focuses on assessing the impact of online health-related videos, articles, and forums on community health, particularly in areas with limited access to healthcare facilities. This study utilizes a dataset of 1.5 million Reddit posts and 750 million YouTube comments to analyze the effectiveness of online discussions in preventing the spread of diseases during the 2014-2018 Ebola outbreak in West Africa. The results show that community engagement and discussion on social media can significantly contribute to preventing disease outbreaks by providing timely and accurate information, thereby reducing the effectiveness of public health interventions. This study highlights the potential of using online data to evaluate the impact of public health interventions and community behaviors, particularly in areas with limited access to healthcare facilities.

The widespread use of the internet has led to an explosion of high-quality image data, but this has been hindered by the limitations of traditional image compression methods, which lack the ability to adapt to changing network conditions and lack the ability to compress images in real-time. Moreover, there is an increasing need for more efficient image compression methods that minimize loss and can be implemented on low-power devices. To address these challenges, we introduce PILC, a novel image compression method that uses an end-to-end neural architecture to learn and adapt to various image types and compression modes. PILC consists of an encoder and decoder, both designed to be efficient on GPUs, and utilizes a unique training approach that allows for real-time evaluation and adjustment of compression performance. Our experimental results demonstrate that PILC outperforms existing image compression methods, achieving higher compression ratios with comparable image quality.

The LHCb experiment has measured the absolute branching fraction of the semileptonic $B^+ \to D_s^+K^+K^-$ decay for the first time, finding it to be $7.2^{+0.5}_{-0.3} \pm 0.6 \pm 0.3 \times 10^{-4}$. This branching fraction is determined using the central value of $R_D$ parameter, which is defined as the ratio of $B^+ \to D_s^+ \mu^+ \nu_\mu$ to $B^+ \to D^+ \mu^+ \nu_\mu$. The measurement of $B^+ \to D_s^+K^+K^-$ decay is the first of its kind and it opens up possibilities for the detection of $B^+ \to D_s^+ \phi$ decay, which is a potential probe for CP violation in the $B$-meson system.

The Gowers approach to ideal transport in stochastic systems involves comparing the rates of change for two coupled systems, with the rate of change in the invariant measure governed by a specific metric that measures how far apart two probability distributions are. However, this approach is sensitive to certain types of anomalies, or anomalies, that can affect the rate of change. In this study, we extend ideal transport theory to systems with continuous time and address the issue of anomalies in this context. We develop a new approach to ideal transport in continuous time and show that it is robust to a specific type of anomaly, demonstrating its applicability to a range of systems including the Lorenz model and a model of interacting particles.

In various scenarios, artificial intelligence agents must collaborate with human partners to achieve shared objectives, but the challenge arises from striking a balance between maximizing one's own rewards and contributing to the overall goal. To tackle this issue, we developed a human choice model that simulates the decision-making process and introduce a method for converting these models into a Markov decision process format. This allows for the training of agents that can work in tandem with humans, using reinforcement learning to optimize their performance. Our model is applied to the classic game of Tetris, where the human player receives a reward-based payoff. Our results show that the agent trained this way excels in a mixed setting against a solitary AI or human teammates in comparison to the other two options.

The concept of supersymmetry relies on a variable with unchanging characteristics, 
a property essential for a consistent and well-defined theoretical framework.
This feature, however, becomes problematic when the variable lacks a predetermined value in a particular model.
This discussion explores the importance of an unchanging supersymmetry parameter in a consistent theoretical description, 
illustrated through a simplified model of a scalar field.
Additionally, we discuss the robustness of supersymmetry in the context of a soft-breaking sector, 
and its implications in the development of a coherent and logical theoretical framework.

This study examines how experts and non-experts perform on various visualization tasks across six tasks, comparing performance among individuals with different levels of spatial skills. Six domains were chosen, each with a unique combination of spatial training. Our findings revealed that expertise and spatial skills had a more significant impact on performance than the specific domain. Notably, individuals with higher spatial skills outperformed those with lower skills by 30-40%, with the spatial skills required varying between 3.0 and 4.0 years apart. Furthermore, experts excelled at all tasks, demonstrating a significant advantage over non-experts. Interestingly, performance varied across tasks, with some tasks showing a greater impact of spatial skills and others showing a lesser effect. Our results suggest that spatial skills are crucial for visualization performance and that creating visualizations for specific domains may not be the most effective way to improve performance.

We introduce a novel category of loops called clause set loops, which are defined within a vector space framework using clause sets from logic that have been normalised through tautology elimination. It's proven that if a vector space loop exists, it's equivalent to a linear loop. Additionally, for specific logic systems, we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions under which vector space loops can be established. Notably, we find that clause set loops can be defined for various logic systems, including linear logic and untyped lambda calculus.

In many machine learning applications, certain data is represented as graphs, 
which necessitates the identification and extraction of subgraphs. This process 
is critical in downstream tasks and is a crucial component of graph neural 
networks. A new algorithm for extracting subgraphs within a larger graph has 
been developed, which involves defining a distance metric between models that 
predict the likelihood of a subgraph being present in the graph. This 
distance measure is based on the gradient of a loss function that assesses 
the model's performance on a training dataset. This gradient is calculated by 
considering the probability distributions of a subgraph within the graph, 
which is determined by the model. The new algorithm leverages the gradient to 
align the probability distributions of a model with a known subgraph, and then 
extracts the subgraph. This approach is more efficient and effective than other 
methods that rely on sampling or optimization algorithms. The new algorithm has 
been successfully applied to models that predict the likelihood of a subgraph 
being present in the graph, and has been compared to other methods that rely 
on optimization or sampling.

Deep learning models are commonly used to model the short-term behavior of neural mass models, yet these models are not well-suited for simulating longer-term dynamics. To address this limitation, a novel approach has been developed that leverages techniques from NLP to improve the model's long-term forecasting capabilities. This approach involves using a combination of two methods - one that uses a single neural network to simulate the evolution of a single neural mass model, and another that uses an ensemble of neural networks to capture the variability in simulations of the same model. The techniques employed include a combination of supervised and self-supervised learning, the use of specialized data augmentation methods, and the incorporation of temporal convolutional and recurrent neural networks to capture the variability in simulations. The results show that these techniques significantly outperform traditional methods in simulating long-term dynamics, and can be easily adapted for simulating other types of neural mass models.

The allocation of power resources among multiple parties is a critical issue, particularly in situations involving power distribution or power sharing agreements. In this research, we explore methods for dividing a given amount of power among multiple parties in a fair and balanced manner, ensuring that the total amount of power allocated equals the total available. We introduce a novel algorithm capable of dividing power among three or more parties and present several variants that fulfill additional requirements or possess specific desirable characteristics.

A significant challenge in processing short, contentious texts is coreference resolution, as identifying entities and the relationships between them is complicated by the lack of context and the prevalence of ambiguous names and descriptions. We focus on a specific type of coreference problem - identifying occurrence coreferences, where the focus is on events rather than entities, and the relationships involve location and timing. We address this issue by developing a novel approach that incorporates both graph-based attention mechanisms and multi-modal information, and our approach outperforms existing methods on a newly created dataset of contentious political events.

This research introduces a revised categorization system for constraints within the Complementarity Knapsack Problem framework, breaking down constraints into distinct classes of continuous and integer variables. The resulting novel categorization enables a more nuanced understanding of constraint types and their impact on Complementarity KSP solutions, including the identification of closed-form solutions and associated constraint families.

This paper defines and analyzes the $f\left(X\right)$-Jordan derivation and $f\left(X\right)$-Jordan centralizer of a semiprime algebra, investigating their properties and characterizations, particularly in relation to the function $f\left(X\right)$. We demonstrate that any $f\left(X\right)$-Jordan derivation of a semiprime algebra is a Jordan derivation, and identify the conditions under which an $f\left(X\right)$-Jordan centralizer behaves like a Jordan centralizer. Our results have implications for nonassociative algebras, and provide novel insights into the function $f(X)=1$ in the context of prime algebras.

We reconcile Weinberg's 2-parameter QFT axioms with helicity constraints from scattering amplitudes in a massless theory with $d \geq 4$. This reveals the source of the two parameters as stemming from angular momentum conservation at the tree level, which necessitates the existence of these parameters to ensure the finiteness of the S-matrix.

We are focusing on a specific type of nonlinear transformations that act on a particular set in $\mathbb{R}^d$. This set is closed under the transformation and is defined as the set of all points that satisfy a specific inequality. The purpose of this research is to investigate the properties of these transformations and to examine their relationship with a specific concept known as transversal groups. This concept refers to the set of all possible transformations that move certain points to each other. We also explore the connection between these transformations and a specific mathematical concept known as Favard length, which is a measure of the distance between certain points in a given set.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to directed policy search that is both computationally efficient and robust in dynamic environments. By leveraging the tube model predictive control's resilience, our approach takes advantage of its properties to develop a policy search method that is resilient to uncertainty as well.
